extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners interested in the science of laughter and humor (psychologists, neuroscientists, sociolinguists, and performers/comedians)
extracted.subtask_description: Assess whether a joke or humorous act will elicit laughter based on social, affiliative, contagion, performer, audience, and phonetic cues rather than on content alone. Emphasizes social dynamics (in-group bonding, shared cues, contagion) and acoustic/authenticity features of laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is the joke designed to bond an in-group?
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the joke designed to bond an in-group?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the joke's content, targets, references, or delivery signal shared identity or group membership. In-group bonding increases the likelihood of laughter because laughter functions as an affiliation signal (agreement, empathy, belonging). Consider whether the joke relies on shared knowledge, insider references, status relations, or identity markers that will be recognized and accepted by the target audience. Anti-pattern: relying on universal or decontextualized punchlines when the aim is to create in-group affiliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does it land in a social context (vs. read alone)?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does it land in a social context (vs. read alone)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most laughter occurs during social interactions rather than in solitary reading; jokes presented where others are present (conversational settings, live audiences, groups) have higher probability of eliciting laughter. Assess the delivery environment: live, group, and conversational contexts amplify laughter; solitary consumption reduces it. Practical implication: prefer interactive or group delivery to maximize laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the comedian's laugh/smile invite audience to join?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the comedian's laugh / smile invite audience to join?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Performers who model affiliative signals (laughing, smiling, inviting cues) encourage audience participation. Speakers themselves produce more laughter (speakers laugh ~46% more than listeners), so a performer's affiliative displays can prime the audience. Consider timing and authenticity of the performer's laugh/smile; forced or poorly timed invitations can backfire. Example: a genuine chuckle that overlaps with the punchline invites contagion; an ostentatious fake laugh may be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the audience already share affiliation cues with the joke?
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the audience already share affiliation cues with the joke?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether audience members have preexisting social ties, shared attitudes, or membership cues that make them receptive. Shared affiliation cues—mutual gaze, common status signals, known shared beliefs—increase the chance that laughter will be used as an affiliation signal. If affiliation cues are absent, the same joke is less likely to produce laughter. Use knowledge of audience demographics, relationships, and subcultural markers when crafting or selecting material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Is contagion possible (others laughing nearby)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter is highly contagious via mirroring and facial mimicry; proximity and visible/audible laughter from others increase the likelihood that additional listeners will laugh. Evaluate seating, audience density, microphone/sound amplification, and whether there are social 'seeds' (early laughers) who can trigger cascades. Practical tactic: foster early, visible laughter (e.g., through supportive audience members, timing) to exploit contagion dynamics. Anti-pattern: isolated individuals or dispersed audiences reduce contagion potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phonetics and authenticity of laughter (timing, vowel quality, faking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Phonetics of laughter: 'ha-ha-ha' shows regular spacing (~210 ms); variation between 'ha' and 'ho' signals emotional valence; hard to fake convincingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the acoustic properties and perceived authenticity of laughter. Timing (regular inter‑laugh intervals ~210 ms) and vowel quality provide cues to genuine affect and valence. Fake laughter often fails to reproduce natural timing and spectral qualities and is therefore less effective at eliciting affiliative responses. For performers or producers: aim for natural-sounding laughter, match rhythm to conversational pacing, and avoid obviously acted laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker/listener dynamics and demographic patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Speakers laugh more than listeners (~46% more); female speakers laugh more than male; female listeners laugh much more at male speakers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating likelihood of laughter, consider who is speaking and who is listening. Speakers' laughter has outsized influence; gendered patterns affect interactional responses and expectations. Use these dynamics to predict which performer–audience pairings or delivery styles will be most effective. Note these are empirical tendencies, not deterministic rules; contextual moderation (topic, audience composition) still matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as 'grooming at a distance' (scaling social bonding)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter functions like primate grooming but at scale, enabling larger group bonding (provides ~3× increase in grouping size compared to one-on-one grooming).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the joke/delivery supports broader social bonding beyond dyadic affiliation. Material and delivery that promote shared laughter can serve as efficient 'grooming' for groups, helping create or maintain cohesive social networks. This criterion matters when the goal is to build group-level affiliation (e.g., community events, team-building, ensemble comedy) rather than only to elicit isolated amusement.
